Learning Objectives
Describe the standard approach for and steps associated with the physical examination of a
patient with a spinal disorder.
Review the anatomic dermatome and myotome distributions of the trunk, pelvis, and upper
and lower extremities.
Understand indications for special examination maneuvers during physical examination of the
spine.
Discuss the implications of positive findings with special examination maneuvers during an
evaluation of the spine.
Overview

The physical examination should be tailored to complement a patient’s history, primary
complaint(s), and symptoms.
Specific neurologic changes that may be related to a spinal origin should be sought.

General Principles
The overarching goal of the physical examination is to correlate findings with a patient’s
complaints and localize a potential etiology or plausible sources for symptoms, which
may direct additional diagnostic approaches, including the need for advanced imaging
studies (eg, MRI or CT). An effective physical examination also allows for the
development of a differential diagnosis. In the outpatient setting, an emphasis generally
is placed on provocative tests that can reproduce symptoms.
The physical examination of the spine should follow the usual pattern of orthopaedic
examinations, with attention paid to inspection of relevant body parts, palpation of
relevant structures, assessment of range of motion, specific/more extensive neurologic
examination, and provocative tests. Provocative tests should be reserved for the end of
the evaluation, especially if anticipated to exacerbate a patient’s pain or symptoms.
Draping/Patient Positioning
The patient should be examined in a gown or other loose-fitting clothing that will
accommodate a complete physical examination, including inspection of the spinal structures.
Patient positioning, draping, and gowning should always be conducted in a manner that
maximizes patient comfort and privacy.

Draping/Patient Positioning
Classically, the patient is in a gown or other loose-fitting clothing that will accommodate
a complete physical examination, including inspection of the spinal structures. Ideally,
the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions are visible through a gown that opens in the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
2/36

back. Patient positioning for the physical examination often involves sitting, standing,
and supine positions. Certain maneuvers may require the patient to be placed in the
prone position. Regardless of patient positioning, draping and gowning should always be
conducted in a manner that maximizes patient comfort and privacy.
General Inspection
Inspection of the Spinal Column and Extremities
Inspection of the spinal column includes evaluation of alignment, the spinal regions, and the
skin.
Evaluation of the extremities includes assessment of the skin, musculature, and any unusual
positioning of the limb or fingers.
Intrinsic wasting and involuntary finger abduction may be observed in patients with chronic
cervical myelopathy.

Inspection of the Spinal Column and Extremities
Typical sagittal alignment of the spine consists of lordosis in the cervical and lumbar
regions and kyphosis in the thoracic and sacrococcygeal regions. The patient should be
viewed from the front and back to assess for asymmetry in anatomic structures in these
regions. Prominence of the scapula or rib cage may indicate underlying scoliosis.
Thoracic kyphosis may manifest as rounded shoulders with an accentuated forward
protrusion of the head and neck when viewed from the side. Abnormal cervical
positioning, such as that which may occur with torticollis, also may be observed. Some
patients with radicular symptoms may stand with the torso shifted away from the
affected extremity, which is so-called sciatic list.
The skin over the spinal structures should be examined for cafe-au-lait spots (indicates
neurofibromatosis), hairy patches (which may represent diastematomyelia), and surgical
scars (size, location, and healing).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
3/36

Visual inspection of the extremities should include evaluation for muscle bulk in the
extremities and any wasting, especially in the hands. Focal muscle wasting in the upper
or lower extremities may indicate chronic radicular or myelopathic processes. For
example, shoulder girdle wasting may indicate a C5 or C6 pathologic process. Intrinsic
wasting of the muscles of the hand is classically referred to as myelopathy of the hand.
This finding may indicate long-standing cervical stenosis and myelopathy. Myelopathy of
the hand also may manifest as passive or spontaneous abduction of the little finger.
However, this is not a specific finding and also may be observed in patients with ulnar
nerve palsy or cubital tunnel syndrome. Similarly, calf atrophy/wasting may indicate
chronic L5 and/or S1 neuropathy or long-standing nerve root compression at these
levels.
Gait Evaluation
Assessment of Gait
A Trendelenburg or antalgic gait may indicate hip or pelvic dysfunction and radicular
symptoms (Resource 1).
A wide-based, shuffling gait may indicate a neurologic disorder, such as cervical myelopathy or
hydrocephalus.
Parkinsonian/festinating gait

Assessment of Gait
Gait assessment can occur as the patient enters the examination room or formally as
part of the physical examination. Much can be appreciated by observing how a patient
carries the body and limbs while moving about the examination room. A Trendelenburg
or antalgic gait may indicate hip or pelvic dysfunction. However, an antalgic gait also may
be associated with referred back or sacral pain and radicular or neuritic processes
affecting the lower extremities. A broad-based gait or shuffle pattern and the need for
visual lower extremity placement may indicate central neurologic disorders, such as
hydrocephalus or cervical myelopathy. Other gait patterns, such as a Parkinsonian or
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
4/36

festinating pattern, may indicate non-spinal etiologies. Patients with a Parkinsonian gait
use a flatfoot strike and may manifest intermittent freezing.
Palpation
Assessment for tenderness over prominent structures in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar
region, including the paraspinal musculature, with notation of any trigger points
Palpation of common peripheral pain generators, such as the shoulders, iliac crests, and hips,
also may be useful.
Anatomic landmarks should be used to reference approximate locations of the most
substantial pain elicited via palpation in the spinal column.

Palpation
Palpation should begin with an evaluation for point tenderness across the spinous
processes, beginning at the occiput and moving the fingers distally across the spinous
processes of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine. Special attention should be paid to
the region or regions most likely associated with a patient’s presenting complaint. For
example, if a patient has complaints associated with a cervical radicular issue, special
attention should be paid to palpation of the spinal structures in the cervical region.
Palpation should assess for tenderness over the cervical facet joints, subaxial paraspinal
musculature, and trapezius as well as the periscapular paraspinal musculature in the
thoracic spine, with notation of any trigger points. Note that cervical facet–mediated pain
may be referred to the trapezial region, the periscapular paraspinal musculature, or the
shoulder region.
Next, palpation should move laterally to the paraspinal musculature at the
costovertebral junction in the thoracic spine and across the facet joints in the lumbar
spine. This is followed by palpation of the sacroiliac joints and the posterior superior iliac
spines for point tenderness. Palpation of the iliac crests, greater trochanters, and ischial
tuberosities to elicit pain may help narrow the differential diagnosis to spinal pain
generators rather than peripheral pain generators. Similarly, axial loading of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
5/36

shoulders during palpation may elicit symptoms associated with dynamic processes or
acute injuries.
In patients with thoracic kyphosis, which may be postural or fixed, surgeons should
determine whether a deformity identified on initial inspection can be passively corrected
via gentle manipulation. Postural kyphosis may be partially passively correctable in many
patients, whereas kyphotic deformities resulting from chronic compression fractures are
not correctable.
For regions in which superficial palpation results in pain, changing palpation technique
may provide additional insight with regard to the source of the pain. For example,
percussive tenderness often indicates recent trauma and may help differentiate an acute
fracture from a chronic fracture (eg, vertebral compression fracture).
Anatomic landmarks should be used to reference approximate locations of the most
substantial pain elicited via palpation. Landmarks may help delineate the anatomic
location of spinal pain.1 The Chassaignac tubercle denotes the C6 level. Given its
location, palpation of the Chassaignac tubercle may be intrinsically uncomfortable. The
vertebra prominens, which is the most prominent spinous process at the base of the
cervical spine, denotes the C7 vertebral level. The scapular spine indicates the T3 level,
whereas the inferior border of the scapulae denotes the T7 level. The superior border of
the iliac is parallel to the L4-5 disk space.
Range of Motion Tests
Range of motion tests are used to assess general range of motion in the spinal segments, to
precipitate or reproduce symptoms, and to evaluate the extent to which peripheral joints may
be contributing to the overall constellation of symptoms.
Motion varies substantially by spinal region.
Cervical spine: flexion/extension, lateral bending, rotation
Thoracic spine: very limited intrinsic motion because of the ribs and sternum
Lumbar spine: flexion/extension and lateral bending
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
6/36


Range of Motion Tests
Range of motion tests are used to assess general range of motion in the spinal
segments, to precipitate or reproduce symptoms, and to evaluate the extent to which
peripheral joints may be contributing to the overall constellation of symptoms. The focus
of range of motion tests should be on the areas of the spine and body that correlate with
the patient’s chief complaint and associated symptoms. Cervical and lumbar range of
motion should be assessed in flexion, in extension, in rotation, and with lateral bending.
Any of these maneuvers may reproduce symptoms. Restrictions in range of motion and
whether restrictions are passive or active in nature also should be noted. Limitations in
range of motion and reproduction of symptoms with attempted range of motion should
be documented.
Motion may be described relative to degrees of rotation or the distance from a
predetermined location (eg, distance between the chin and chest on forward flexion). At
a minimum, patients should be asked to flex and extend the cervical spine, rotate the
neck from one side to the other, and flex and extend at the lumbosacral junction. A
spinal curve examination can be performed during forward flexion at the lumbosacral
junction or during flexion of the trunk. Surgeons should evaluate for rib or scapular
prominence during these maneuvers (Resource 2).
Assessment of pain with range of motion of peripheral joints can be performed as
necessary. Reproduction of pain with passive or active range of motion of the hips,
knees, and shoulders may direct attention to these joints as primary or secondary pain
generators relative to spinal structures.
Provocative Tests and Special Maneuvers
Provocative tests help differentiate spinal pathology from other musculoskeletal conditions.
Typically, provocative maneuvers should be performed at the end of the general physical
examination if anticipated to elucidate substantial amounts of pain.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
7/36

Special maneuvers are best used to further narrow the differential diagnosis of spinal
disorders that align with a patient’s symptoms.

Provocative Tests and Special Maneuvers
Provocative tests help differentiate spinal pathology from other musculoskeletal
conditions and pathology, including those involving peripheral joints or myofascial
structures. Provocative maneuvers should be performed at the end of the general
physical examination if anticipated to elucidate substantial amounts of pain or
discomfort. These special maneuvers are best used to further narrow the differential
diagnosis of spinal disorders that align with a patient’s symptoms.
Tests for Cervical Spine Pathology
The Spurling maneuver and the look-away test are provocative tests for radicular symptoms.
The over-the-head relief sign, or Bakody sign, is a reliving measure for radicular symptoms.
Lhermitte sign for myelopathy

Tests for Cervical Spine Pathology
Several maneuvers can be used to elucidate the etiology of symptoms in the cervical
spine region and the upper extremities. The most common provocative test for cervical
radicular symptoms is the Spurling maneuver (Figure 1). The Spurling maneuver may
elicit symptoms associated with nerve root compression in the lateral recess and/or
foraminal zone, indicating a radicular process. The Spurling maneuver is performed by
applying an axial load to the neck while it is rotated toward the side of the pathology and
in extension. The Spurling maneuver is positive if it re-creates radicular symptoms, which
may consist of pain, numbness, tingling, or paresthesias in an appropriate distribution.1
These findings should occur ipsilateral to the lesion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
8/36

Figure 1 Illustration shows the Spurling maneuver. (Reproduced from Hilibrand AS:
Physical examination of the spine, in in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020, pp 106-114.)
The look-away test is similar to the Spurling maneuver and produces similar findings.
The look-away test is performed via passive abduction of the affected extremity at the
shoulder with extension at the elbow and wrist.1 The patient is instructed to turn the
head away from the affected extremity. Reproduction of radicular symptoms, including
pain, numbness, tingling, or paresthesias, in an appropriate distribution is considered a
positive test. Patients who display guarding during attempts to perform the Spurling
maneuver may benefit from assessment via the look-away test.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
9/36

The over-the-head relief sign, or Bakody sign, is assessed by passively or actively having
the patient drape the affected extremity over the head with flexion at the elbow (Figure
2). This maneuver potentially decompresses the neural foramen on the affected side. A
decrease or resolution of symptoms with this maneuver represents a positive finding.2
Figure 2 Clinical photograph of a patient exhibiting the over-the-head relief sign, or
Bakody sign. By placing her hand on top of her head, this patient lessens tension on the
cervical nerve roots, which decreases pain in her right extremity. (Reproduced from
Metzler JP: Physical examination in spine care, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 63-72.)
The Lhermitte sign is assessed in patients in whom cervical stenosis and myelopathy are
suspected. The Lhermitte sign is assessed by bringing the neck into flexion or extension
and providing an axial load. This maneuver usually is performed with flexion. Shock-like
sensations radiating down the spinal axis into the arms and/or legs is considered a
positive finding and results from stretching and direct compression of the spinal cord in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
10/36

a stenotic canal. The Lhermitte sign is classically encountered in patients with cervical
myelopathy. The Lhermitte sign is specific but not sensitive for the diagnosis of
myelopathy.2 Similarly, the Lhermitte sign is not specific or sensitive for the diagnosis of
cervical radiculopathy. The maneuver may lead to positive findings in patients with
multiple sclerosis or vitamin B12 deficiency.
In patients with facet-mediated neck pain, extension and axial loading of the head may
exacerbate subaxial pain and reproduce pain in the cervical cape or referred pain zones
associated with the facet joints. Pain exacerbation or the reproduction of symptoms is
considered a positive finding.
Impingement tests and focused, active/passive evaluation of the shoulder are used as
supplemental examination maneuvers to rule out intrinsic shoulder pathology if
indicated. Similarly, the Phalen maneuver and the Tinel sign are used to rule out carpal
tunnel syndrome at the wrist if concern for double crush phenomenon or symptomatic
overlap exists. Likewise, percussion of the cubital tunnel is used to rule out ulnar
compressive neuropathy.
Tests for Lumbar Spine Pathology
Dural tension signs, such as the straight leg raise test, Lasègue sign, slump test, and femoral
nerve stretch test, are used to assess for nerve compression in the lumbar spine.

Tests for Lumbar Spine Pathology
The straight leg raise test can be performed with the patient in a seated or supine
position2 (Figure 3). With the hip flexed and the knee extended, the leg is raised to an
angle of 70° to 90°. The reproduction of radiating leg pain (below the knee) in a
dermatomal distribution with hip flexion near 90° and the knee extended is highly
sensitive for nerve root compression by a herniated disk at L4-5 or L5-S1. This straight
leg raise test is considered sensitive (approximately 90%) for the detection of radicular
pain but is not specific for the diagnosis of a disk herniation. The straight leg raise test
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
11/36

may be positive in patients with other sources of nerve compression, such as spondylotic
spinal stenosis, a fracture, or metastatic epidural compression.
Figure 3 Illustrations show the straight leg raise test. (Reproduced from Hilibrand AS:
Physical examination of the spine, in in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020, pp 106-114.)
The crossed straight leg raise test can be used as a supplemental test and may be
positive in patients with a very large disk herniation.1 During the crossed straight leg
raise test, passive extension of the contralateral leg via a technique similar to that used
during the straight leg raise test produces pain radiating down the symptomatic leg. A
positive crossed straight leg raise test is very specific (90%) for the diagnosis of a
contralaterally herniated disk.
The Lasègue sign (Bowstring test) may be used in combination with the straight leg raise.
During the Bowstring test, the leg is brought toward 90° with maintenance of some knee
flexion. As the patient begins to experience pain with passive flexion of the hip, flexion is
stopped, and the knee is extended further in combination with passive dorsiflexion of
the ankle. The Bowstring test is considered positive if this last maneuver replicates the
pain radiating down the leg. The Bowstring test should mirror the findings of the straight
leg raise test.
The slump test is another corollary to the straight leg raise test (Figure 4). The slump test
is performed with the patient in a seated position with the shoulders rounded and the
trunk and neck flexed.3 The affected extremity is evaluated via a straight leg raise
maneuver. Reproduction of radicular symptoms represents a positive finding. The slump
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
12/36

test is the most sensitive of the three maneuvers performed to evaluate dural tension in
the lower extremity (eg, straight leg raise test, Lasègue sign, slump test; Resource 3). If
the straight leg raise test is positive, then all three of these maneuvers do not have to be
performed. However, patients with a positive straight leg raise test should have similar
results on the Bowstring test and the slump test. Discrepancies between these tests may
indicate other pain generators or evaluation for nonorganic findings.
Figure 4 Clinical photograph shows the seated slump test. To maximize tension on the
L5 and S1 nerve roots, the seated patient is asked to slump forward. The symptomatic
lower extremity then is extended, and the ankle is dorsiflexed. Reproduction of the
patient’s typical pain or paresthesias is considered a positive test. (Reproduced from
Metzler JP: Physical examination in spine care, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 63-72.)
The aforementioned dural tension tests only evaluate the lower nerve root distributions
of the lumbar spine, typically L4-S1. The femoral nerve stretch test is an analogous
maneuver to evaluate for radicular findings in the proximal lumbar distributions (Figure
5). The patient is placed in the prone position, the hip is extended, and the knee is

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
13/36

flexed. The femoral nerve stretch test is a provocative test, placing tension on the upper
lumbar roots and creating a concordant radiculopathy. Reproduction of symptoms with
knee flexion and hip extension is highly sensitive for the diagnosis of a herniated disk at
L2-3 or L1-2.
The Hoover test is performed if concern exists with regard to a patient’s level of
participation in the physical examination. The examiner cups both heels of the patient,
who is in the supine position, and elevates them slightly off the examination table. The
patient is then asked to actively raise each leg (one at a time) off the examiner’s hands.
The examiner should experience a downward pressure on the contralateral side as the
patient attempts to elevate the opposite leg. A positive finding occurs if no such
downward pressure is encountered, indicating incomplete participation by the patient. A
positive result should indicate evaluation for other pain generators, including possible
nonorganic pain generators (Waddell signs).
Figure 5 Clinical photograph shows the femoral nerve stretch test. The L2 through L4
nerve roots are stretched by placing the patient in the prone position and then flexing
the knee and extending the hip. Reproduction of the patient’s typical pain or
paresthesias is considered a positive test. (Reproduced from Metzler JP: Physical

examination in spine care, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 63-72.)
Tests for Pelvic and Sacral Pathology
Patients and providers often mistake symptoms from the hip and sacroiliac region as being
derived from the spine.
If indicated, adjunct testing of the hips and pelvic structures should be performed to rule out
intrinsic pathology and/or manifestations of hip-spine syndrome.

Tests for Pelvic and Sacral Pathology
Patients and providers often mistake symptoms from the hip and sacroiliac region as
being derived from the spine and vice versa. If indicated, adjunct testing of the hips and
pelvic structures should be performed to rule out intrinsic pathology and/or
manifestations of hip-spine syndrome. To rule out osteoarthritis of the hip, the hip
should be passively brought through internal and external rotation, assessing for
substantial restriction of motion (especially on internal rotation). To rule out sacroiliac-
mediated pain, a focused examination of the sacroiliac joints should be performed
(Figure 6), including the FABER (flexion, abduction and external rotation) test and/or the
Gaenslen test. The FABER test is performed with the patient in a seated position or the
supine position.2 In patients with sacroiliitis or joint dysfunction, the FABER test should
reproduce symptoms in the sacroiliac region. The FABER test also may reproduce hip-
related symptoms that manifest as groin pain or pain radiating along the medial thigh to
the knee. The Gaenslen test is performed with the patient in the supine position on the
examination table with both legs flexed to the chest and the affected buttock
unsupported on the examination table. The examiner drops the affected/unsupported
leg and extends the hip. A positive finding is considered the reproduction of pain at the
affected sacroiliac joint. The Gaenslen test is more difficult for the patient and the
examiner than the FABER test and may not be necessary in patients with a positive
FABER test.

AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074

Figure 6 Clinical photographs show sacroiliac joint provocation tests. Reproduction of
the patient’s typical pain is considered a positive test. A, The distraction test. With the
patient in the supine position, the examiner’s hands are placed on the anterior superior
iliac spine of each ilia, and a lateral and posterior force is applied. B, The thigh thrust
test. With the patient in the supine position and the hip flexed to 90°, a posteriorly
directed force is applied to the femur, placing a shearing stress on the sacroiliac joint. C,
The compression test. The patient lies on the asymptomatic side, and the examiner
places pressure on the superior iliac crest, directing it toward the opposite iliac crest. D,
The sacral thrust test. With the patient in the prone position and the ilia fixed against the
examination table, the examiner’s hand is placed in the center of the sacrum, and an
anteriorly directed force is applied. (Reproduced from Metzler JP: Physical examination in
spine care, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 63-72.)
Neurologic Examination
Surgeons must be familiar with the dermatomal patterns of the trunk, pelvis, upper
extremities, and lower extremities to perform an effective spinal evaluation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
16/36


Neurologic Examination
The neurologic examination should focus on dermatomes in the upper and lower
extremities and should include various sensory and motor tests as week as the
assessment of reflexes and gait as appropriate. Pressure and sensation to touch can be
assessed with the use of a cotton tipped applicator, with the use of a device similar to a
cotton tipped applicator, or manually. Typically, vibration, proprioception, and
temperature sensation are assessed as adjuncts if concern for a central nervous system
lesion or disorder exists. Placement of a tuning fork at the distal joints or over
dermatomal distributions in the lower extremities may help identify peripheral
neuropathy, especially relative to diabetes mellitus.
Sensory Examination
Typically, bilateral sensory testing is performed to assess the C5-T1 dermatomes in the upper
extremities and the L1-S1 dermatomes in the lower extremities. The T2-T12 dermatomes may
be evaluated as necessary over the trunk, back, and abdomen.

Sensory Examination
The sensory examination should be performed bilaterally for comparison with the
unaffected extremity, if possible, and to evaluate for symmetry. Typically, bilateral
sensory testing is performed to assess the C5-T1 dermatomes in the upper extremities
and the L1-S1 dermatomes in the lower extremities. The T2-T12 dermatomes may be
evaluated as necessary over the trunk, back, and abdomen. Dermatomal distributions
may overlap, and some degree of individual variation exists (Figure 7). Common
landmarks for the sensory examination include the C4 dermatome, acromioclavicular
joint; T4 dermatome, chest wall at the level of the nipples; T7 dermatome, chest wall at
the level of the xiphoid process; T10 dermatome, abdominal wall at the level of the
umbilicus; T12 dermatome, abdominal wall at the level of the inguinal crease; and S3, S4,
and S5 dermatomes, skin around the perianal region. The C4 dermatome may run low

AAOS | Physical Examination of the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074
17/36

on the chest, confusing the interpretation of physical examination results in patients
with a complete injury to the spinal cord at the cervical level.
Figure 7 Illustrations show the sensory dermatomes of the upper (A) and lower (B)
extremities. (Reproduced with permission from Klein JD, Garfin SR: Clinical evaluation of
patients with suspected spine problems, in Frymoyer JW, Ducker TB, Hadler NM, Kostuik
JP, Weinstein JN, Whitecloud TS III, eds: The Adult Spine: Principles and Practice, ed 2.
Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott-Raven, 1997, p 320.)
Motor Examination and Strength Testing
Testing specific myotome distributions allows the examiner to correlate patient-reported
symptoms with potential pathology derived from specific spinal levels.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:24 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001074

Typically, upper extremity testing involves assessment of the muscles innervated by the nerves
from C5 through T1. In general, lower extremity testing involves assessment of the muscles
innervated by the nerves with roots from L2 through S1.

Motor Examination and Strength Testing
Testing specific myotome distributions allows the examiner to correlate patient-reported
symptoms with potential pathology derived from specific spinal levels. Motor findings
attributable to a myotome may be more discrete on examination than objective sensory
changes or subjective patient complaints of paresthesias in nonspecific or overlapping
distributions. Typically, upper extremity testing involves assessment of the muscles
innervated by the nerves from C5 through T1 (Figure 8). In general, lower extremity
testing involves assessment of the muscles innervated by the nerves with roots from L2
through S1 (Figure 9).

Myotome Evaluation
Myotomes can be evaluated efficiently via simple tests from C5-T1 and L2-S1.

Myotome Evaluation
Myotomes in the upper extremity can be evaluated efficiently via the following tests: C5,
testing the deltoid with shoulder abduction; C6, wrist extension; C7, triceps extension,
wrist flexion, and finger extension; C8, finger flexors; and T1, intrinsic muscles of the
hand (finger abduction and adduction).4 Myotomes in the lower extremity can be
evaluated efficiently via the following tests: L2, hip flexion; L3, knee extension; L4, ankle
dorsiflexion; L5, great toe dorsiflexion; and S1, ankle plantar flexion
Grading of Manual Muscle Testing
Motor testing is graded using a common scale ranging from 0/5 to 5/5.
If a patient complies with a complete examination and demonstrates no deficits, then a grade
of normal strength (5/5) is applied to each level.

Grading of Manual Muscle Testing
Muscle testing should be assessed bilaterally if possible. Performance on the affected
side should be compared with that of the unaffected side to determine a grade. If a
patient complies with a complete examination and demonstrates no deficits, then a
grade of normal strength (5/5) is applied. Motor testing is graded using the following
scale: grade 5/5, full strength with the ability resist examiner attempts to move the limb
or joint in question; grade 4/5, limited ability resist examiner attempts to move the limb
or joint in question; grade 3/5, movement against gravity alone with no ability to resist

Gait Testing
Gait testing may afford additional insight with regard to the source of spinal pathology and
may help identify mimics of spinal pathology, such as peripheral joint issues and central
nervous system disorders (Resource 1).
Typically, gait testing is performed in an office setting and includes the tandem gait test,
Romberg test, and single leg stance test, as well as heel walking and toe walking.

Gait Testing
Patients may be asked to perform specific gait maneuvers to further elucidate spinal
pathology. Gait and stance testing may afford additional insight with regard to
myelopathic or radicular processes. Coordination issues or involuntary movements in
combination with a shuffle gait and rigidity may indicate other neurologic disorders.
Typically, gait testing is performed in an office setting and includes the tandem gait test,
Romberg test, and single leg stance test, as well as heel walking and toe walking.1,2
During the tandem gait test, the patient is asked to walk to the opposite side of the
room, turn around to face the examiner, and walk toward the examiner, placing one foot
in front of the other and touching heel to toe. The patient should be observed for loss of
balance, inaccurate foot placement, and lack of coordination. Patients with advanced
cervical myelopathy may have difficulty performing the tandem gait test. Other
conditions that may cause difficulty during the tandem gait test include osteoarthritis of
the hips and knees, upper motor neuron disorders, and vestibular dysfunction. The
Romberg test is commonly performed with the patient standing erect with the feet
together, arms in front, and eyes closed. The patient should be observed for any
swaying. Inability to resist swaying and loss of coordination may indicate central nervous
system or vestibular issues.

For heel walking and toe walking, the patient is observed while walking on the heels and
then while walking on the toes. These tests will be abnormal if any substantial weakness
in the tibialis anterior muscle (difficulties with heel walking) or the gastrocnemius-soleus
complex (difficulties with toe walking) is present. Such findings may indicate central
nervous system pathology and long-standing spinal-related issues, such as chronic
severe stenosis. During the single leg stance test, the patient is asked to stand on one leg
at a time. The hips should remain balanced as the patient performs this maneuver. A
drop of one side may indicate gluteus medius weakness (L5 nerve); however, this finding
is nonspecific because it may be the result of multiple causes.
Rectal Examination
Not routinely performed in the office setting unless a clear indication
A rectal examination includes assessment for anal wink, evaluation of rectal tone, and
evaluation for the bulbocavernosus reflex as indicated.

Rectal Examination
A rectal examination is not routinely performed in the outpatient setting but is indicated
in patients with a traumatic injury, patients with any bowel or bladder dysfunction, and
patients in whom upper motor neuron disease is suspected. Key elements of a rectal
examination include assessment for anal wink, evaluation of rectal tone, and evaluation
for the bulbocavernosus reflex. Evaluation for the bulbocavernosus reflex is particularly
important in patients with a spinal cord injury and is most frequently performed in an
inpatient setting.
Assessment for anal wink is a test for the anocutaneous reflex. Gently stroking the
mucocutaneous junction of the circumanal skin results in involuntary contraction of the
external anal sphincter in patients with intact neurologic function. Absence of the
anocutaneous reflex may indicate a spinal cord injury or absent function of the sacral
nerve roots.

Assessment for anal wink is followed by a digital rectal examination and evaluation of

of the mons, which then stimulates tightening of the anal sphincter in patients with

Reflex Testing
Reflex testing incorporates aspects of sensory and motor pathways.
Reflex testing aids in differentiating upper motor neuron disease from lower motor neuron
disease.

Reflex Testing
Reflex testing incorporates aspects of sensory and motor pathways and evaluates
communication between the integrated components of the reflex arc. Reflex testing aids
in the differentiation of upper motor neuron disease from lower motor neuron disease.
Patients with lower motor neuron disorders have diminished reflexes, whereas patients
with upper motor neuron conditions have an exaggerated response. The following
grading scale is used for reflex testing: grade 0, areflexic (absent reflex); grade 1, hypo-
reflexic (diminished reflex); grade 2, normal reflex response; grade 3, hyper-reflexic;
grade 4, hyper-reflexic with clonus. Findings that are causes for concern include
areflexia, reflexes that are asymmetric on the ipsilateral side, and reflexes that are
asymmetric on the contralateral side.
Upper Extremity Reflexes
Reflexes that can be tested in the upper extremity include C5, C6, and C7.

Upper Extremity Reflexes

The biceps reflex, which represents C5, is tested by palpating directly onto the biceps
tendon and striking this area with the use of a reflex hammer. The brachioradialis reflex,
which represents C6, is tested by striking the radial aspect of the forearm with the use of
a reflex hammer. Normal reflex results in radial deviation of the wrist. The triceps reflex,
which represents the C7 reflex arc, is tested by having the patient rest the forearm with
the elbow in a flexed position and striking the triceps tendon with the use of a reflex
hammer.
Lower Extremity Reflexes
Reflexes that can be tested in the lower extremity include L4 and S1.

Lower Extremity Reflexes
The patellar reflex, which represents L4, is tested by striking the patellar tendon with the
use of a reflex hammer with the knee flexed. The Achilles reflex, which represents S1, is
tested by striking the Achilles tendon with the use of a reflex hammer. Normal reflex
results in plantar flexion of the foot. The ankle may need to be flexed as much as 90° for
adequate tension on the Achilles tendon to allow for deformation and a proper reflex
response.
Pathologic Reflexes in the Upper and Lower Extremities
Pathologic reflexes often represent dysfunction of long-tract neural pathways and feature
prominently in the diagnosis of cervical myelopathy.
Pathologic reflex testing includes the Hoffman test, the inverted radial reflex, the Babinski sign,
the Oppenheim sign, and ankle clonus.

Pathologic reflexes often represent dysfunction of long-tract neural pathways and
feature prominently in the diagnosis of cervical myelopathy. Pathologic reflex testing in
the upper extremity includes the Hoffman test and the inverted radial reflex. Pathologic
reflex testing in the lower extremity includes the Babinski sign, the Oppenheim sign, and
ankle clonus.
The Hoffman test is performed by flicking the distal phalanx of the long finger into an
extended position while holding a more proximal portion of the finger. A positive test is
indicated by involuntary flexion of the interphalangeal joint of the ipsilateral thumb.
Alternatively, the Hoffman test can be performed by grasping the distal phalanx of the
long finger and flicking it into an extended position. Involuntary flexion of the
interphalangeal joint of the ipsilateral thumb indicates a positive finding. A positive test
result is sensitive but not specific for the diagnosis of cervical myelopathy.
The inverted radial reflex is assessed via a maneuver performed during the assessment
of the brachioradialis reflex. During testing of the brachioradialis reflex, as already
described, the thumb and fingers flex, and ulnar deviation of the wrist rather than
normal radial deviation occurs. Such findings may indicate upper motor neuron
dysfunction or cervical myelopathy.
The Babinski sign is assessed by stroking the lateral aspect of the plantar portion of the
foot. A positive Babinski sign is indicated by extension of the great toe with splaying of
the smaller toes. This finding should be differentiated from withdrawal, in which the foot
itself withdraws from the stroke but the toes curl downward rather than upward and
outward. A positive Babinski sign may indicate an upper motor neuron disorder.
The Oppenheim sign is an alternative test that results in findings similar to those of the
Babinski sign.1 The Oppenheim sign may be easier to assess in select patients or if
assessment of the Babinski sign results in an equivocal response. The Oppenheim sign is
assessed by firmly running the fingers or a reflex hammer along the tibial crest. A
positive Oppenheim sign leads to extension of the great toe with splaying of the smaller
toes. Similar to a positive Babinski sign, a positive Oppenheim sign may indicate an
upper motor neuron disorder.

The test for ankle clonus is performed with the patient relaxed and in a seated position
or in the supine position. The ankle is dorsiflexed firmly and quickly by the examiner.
Involuntary repeated contraction of the Achilles tendon and the gastrocnemius-soleus
complex for more than five beats and/or a positive Babinski sign is a pathologic finding.
Pathologic ankle clonus may indicate upper motor neuron disease, including cervical
myelopathy.
Other Tests
Waddell Signs
Waddell described five discrete findings concerning for nonorganic pain generation.
Evaluation for Waddell signs may be indicated in patients with a history and physical
examination findings that are discordant with or fail to substantiate the most common
etiologies associated with the constellation of symptoms.

Waddell Signs
Certain patients may have a history, complaints, and physical examination findings that
are not well aligned. In such patients, the history and physical examination findings may
be discordant with or fail to substantiate the most common etiologies associated with
the constellation of symptoms. Such findings indicate the need for additional evaluation
of nonorganic pain generation. Waddell described five discrete findings concerning for
nonorganic pain generation.1,2 These findings, or Waddell signs, include superficial or
nonanatomic tenderness, simulation, an exaggerated pain response, regionalization,
and changes in examination findings with distraction1 (Table 1).

Regionalization is present in patients with complaints of leg numbness or weakness over
the entire leg or in a nonanatomic distribution.
Simulation includes nonanatomic motor and/or sensory impairment and testing areas a
patient perceives as belonging to the spine but do not stress the spinal column. These
tests can be used to further elucidate nonorganic pain generation. Commonly, patients
perceive that these tests place stress on spinal structures; however, they do not involve
the spinal column. For example, simulated rotation of the trunk and waist moves the
body about the hips and knees rather than the spine. Frequently used simulation tests
include axial compression of the head, simulated spinal rotation, and the lumbar roll.
During simulated lumbar rotation, the examiner manipulates the patient’s shoulders or
hips to mimic rotation through the lumbosacral segments. All motion during simulated
lumbar rotation occurs through the knees and hips. No reproduction of back pain or
symptom magnification should occur. Complaints of symptoms during simulated lumbar
rotation suggests non-spinal pathology.
During the axial compression test, the head, shoulders, or heels are gently loaded by the
examiner. No more than 5 lbs of pressure should be applied, which is not enough weight
to affect lumbar spine structures. Reproduction of pain or complaints of symptom
magnification cannot be attributed to lumbar spine structures.
During the lumbar roll, the skin around the oblique musculature is manipulated by the
examiner. This should not result in complaints of back or leg pain. Complaints of
symptoms during the lumbar roll suggests non-spinal pathology.

In patients with Waddell findings associated with distraction, inconsistent complaints of
pain are reported with similar examination maneuvers performed in different manners
or during conversation with subtle testing alone. For example, pain generation should be
the same in patients with radiculopathy in whom the straight leg raise test is performed
in a seated position and in the supine position. Some patients may perceive that a
seated straight leg raise test assesses the knee joint rather than the spine (Figure 10).
The presence of three or more of the five Waddell signs strongly suggests symptom
magnification, nonorganic pain, and illness behavior rather than physical injury or spinal
disease. The Waddell signs are commonly mislabeled as tests for malingering; however,
these signs are not tests for malingering and should not be referred to as such. The
Waddell signs solely indicate the potential for nonorganic sources of pain or nonorganic
components to a patient’s constellation of symptoms.

Typically, supplemental tests are performed if the clinical diagnosis, often a central nervous

Supplemental tests may include assessment for the jaw jerk reflex, testing of the cranial


Supplemental Neurologic Tests
Typically, supplemental tests are performed if the clinical diagnosis, often a central
nervous system issue or myelopathy, remains unclear. Myelopathic findings may not be
grossly evident based on the history or physical examination findings, especially early in
the pathologic process or in patients with myeloradiculopathy, and more subtle testing
may be necessary.
In patients in whom upper motor neuron disease is suspected, testing of cranial nerves
3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 12 may aid in documenting additional deficits. Any deficits in these
nerve distributions cannot be attributed to spinal pathology. In addition, the jaw jerk
reflex may be assessed by downwardly striking the middle of the mandible just above
the chin with the use of a reflex hammer. Rapid opening and closing of the jaw indicates
upper motor neuron dysfunction centered above the level of the spinal cord, such as
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
In patients in whom myelopathy is suspected, coordination tests, such as open-and-
closed hand testing and triangle step testing, may be performed. During the open-and-
closed hand test, the patient is instructed to open and close the hands as quickly as
possible for 20 seconds with the shoulders abducted and the hands held above the
head. Lack of coordination or inability to perform 20 good repetitions in 20 seconds
indicates the need for additional evaluation for myelopathy.
The triangle step test is performed by asking the patient to use the great toe of one foot
to touch three points of an imaginary triangle on the examination room floor as quickly
as possible for 20 seconds (Resource 4). The maneuver should be repeated for each
foot. Lack of coordination or inability to perform 20 good repetitions in 20 seconds
indicates the need for additional evaluation for myelopathy.5 Patients may have difficulty
